languages.name: Old Georgian
languages.note: Written from the 5th century CE; no everyday greeting recorded.

languages.name: Parthian
languages.note: Known from inscriptions and Manichaean texts; no greeting recorded.

languages.name: Phoenician / Punic
languages.note: Known from inscriptions; no greeting recorded.

languages.name: Mycenaean Greek
languages.note: Written in Linear B on administrative tablets; no greeting recorded.

languages.name: Common Brittonic
languages.note: Known from names on coins and Roman records; no greeting recorded.

languages.name: Old Irish
languages.note: Written from the 6th century; no everyday greeting recorded.

languages.name: Pictish
languages.note: Barely attested, mainly in place names; its classification is debated.

languages.name: Old Chinese
languages.note: Written on oracle bones and bronzes; pronunciation is reconstructed.

languages.name: Middle Chinese
languages.note: Pronunciation reconstructed from rhyme dictionaries such as the Qieyun (601 CE).

languages.name: Manchu
languages.note: Co-official in the Qing court; now nearly extinct as a spoken language.

languages.name: Mixe–Zoquean (proto)
languages.note: Proposed language of the Olmec; this attribution is a hypothesis.

hello.note: "what do you say?", a common greeting

languages.name: Otomi
languages.note: Greetings vary widely between Otomi varieties.

languages.name: Zapotec
languages.note: A family of languages; greetings vary by variety.

events: Kura–Araxes settlements spread across the South Caucasus
facts: Its distinctive black-burnished pottery spread from the Caucasus as far as the Levant.
The language its people spoke is unknown; Hurro-Urartian and early Kartvelian are among the guesses.
entities.name: Kura–Araxes culture
entities.summary: The Kura–Araxes culture was an archaeological culture that existed from about 4000 BC until about 2000 BC, which has traditionally been regarded as the date of its end; in some locations it may have disappeared as early as 2600 or 2700 BC. The earliest evidence for this culture is found on the Ararat plain in the Armenian highlands; it spread north in the Caucasus by 3000 BC.

events: Wine is pressed and fermented in Areni-1 cave
A leather shoe is left in Areni-1 cave
Found in 2008; the oldest leather shoe known.
facts: Areni-1 cave holds the oldest known leather shoe, about 5,500 years old.
The same cave contains the oldest known winery, dated to about 4100 BCE.
entities.name: Areni-1 cave communities
entities.summary: The Areni-1 cave complex is an ancient multicomponent site, and late Chalcolithic/Early Bronze Age ritual site and settlement, located near the Areni village in southern Armenia along the Arpa River.

facts: Wooden wagons and chariots from Lchashen, on Lake Sevan, are among the oldest preserved in the world.
Metsamor was a centre of bronze and iron metallurgy.
entities.name: Lchashen–Metsamor culture
entities.summary: Lchashen-Metsamor culture is an archeological culture of the Late Bronze Age and Early Iron Age in the South Caucasus. It was mainly spread in areas of present-day Armenia. Lchashen-Metsamor pottery was also found in the Ağrı Province of Turkey and in southern Georgia.

rulers: Late kings (Sarduri III, Rusa III, Rusa IV)
events: Aramu unites the tribes of the Armenian Highlands
Recorded on a cuneiform foundation inscription found in 1950.
Sargon II of Assyria sacks Musasir
A temple of Ḫaldi is looted; Urartu is weakened.
Probably overrun by the Medes and Scythians.
facts: Urartians called their land Biainili; "Urartu" is the Assyrian name, related to the biblical "Ararat".
The fortress of Erebuni, founded by Argishti I in 782 BCE, is the origin of the city of Yerevan.
Urartian engineers built canals still in use today, such as the Menua (Shamiram) canal near Van.
entities.name: Kingdom of Urartu
entities.summary: Urartu was an ancient civilization and Iron Age kingdom centered on the Armenian highlands between Lake Van, Lake Urmia, and Lake Sevan. The territory of the ancient kingdom of Urartu extended over the modern frontiers of Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Armenia. Its kings left behind cuneiform inscriptions in the Urartian language, a member of the Hurro-Urartian language family.

gov: Province (satrapy) of the Achaemenid Persian Empire
religion: Early Zoroastrian and local Armenian gods
events: Darius I records revolts in Armenia.
facts: The name Armenia ("Armina") first appears in the trilingual Behistun inscription of Darius the Great, c. 520 BCE.
Xenophon passed through in 401 BCE and described Armenian villages with underground houses.
entities.name: Satrapy of Armenia
entities.summary: The Satrapy of Armenia, a region controlled by the Orontid dynasty, was one of the satrapies of the Achaemenid Empire in the 6th century BC that later became an independent kingdom. Its capital were Erebuni.

gov: Monarchy, at times under Seleucid suzerainty
events: Battle of Gaugamela: Persian rule ends
Armenian contingents fought for Darius III.
facts: After Alexander's conquest of Persia, Armenia's Orontid rulers became effectively independent kings.
entities.name: Kingdom of Armenia (Orontid)
entities.summary: The Orontid dynasty, also known as the Eruandids or Eruandunis, ruled the Satrapy of Armenia until 330 BC and the Kingdom of Armenia from 321 BC to 200 BC. The Orontids ruled first as client kings or satraps of the Achaemenid Empire and after the collapse of the Achaemenid Empire established an independent kingdom. Later, a branch of the Orontids ruled as kings of Sophene and Commagene. They are the first of the three royal dynasties that successively ruled the ancient Kingdom of Armenia. Although the overthrow of Orontes IV and the accession of Artaxias I to the throne of Armenia in the early 2nd century BC is traditionally treated as the start of a new dynasty, Artaxias probably belonged to a branch of the Orontid dynasty. His descendants ruled Armenia until the 1st century AD.

rulers: Late Artaxiads under Roman and Parthian pressure
religion: Armenian polytheism (Aramazd, Anahit, Vahagn), with Greek and Iranian influences
events: After the Seleucid defeat at Magnesia (190 BCE).
Ancient sources credit Hannibal with advising on its site.
facts: Artaxias I set up boundary stones inscribed in Aramaic; several have been found in Armenia.
Under Tigranes the Great, Armenia briefly stretched from the Caspian Sea to the Mediterranean.
King Artavasdes II wrote Greek tragedies, according to Plutarch.
entities.name: Kingdom of Armenia (Artaxiad)
entities.summary: The Artaxiad dynasty ruled the Kingdom of Armenia from 189 BC until their overthrow by the Romans in 12 AD. It was founded by Artaxias I, who claimed kinship with the previous ruling dynasty of Armenia, the Orontids. Their realm included Greater Armenia, Sophene and, intermittently, parts of Mesopotamia. Their main enemies were the Romans, the Seleucids and the Parthians, against whom the Armenians conducted multiple wars. Under the Artaxiad king Tigranes the Great, the Kingdom of Armenia reached its greatest territorial extent, extending for a brief period from the Caspian to the Mediterranean Sea.

gov: Monarchy contested between Rome and Persia
events: Nero crowns Tiridates I in Rome
Traditional date; some scholars argue for 314.
One of the oldest cathedrals in the world.
Armenia partitioned between Rome and Persia
Persia receives the larger eastern part.
Armenian alphabet created by Mesrop Mashtots
The Persian king abolishes the Armenian monarchy
facts: Armenia is traditionally the first state to adopt Christianity, in 301 (some historians prefer 314).
Mesrop Mashtots created the 36-letter Armenian alphabet around 405; it is still in use.
Nero crowned Tiridates I in Rome in 66, a famous settlement between Rome and Parthia.
entities.name: Kingdom of Armenia (Arsacid)
entities.summary: The Arsacid dynasty, called the Arshakuni in Armenian, ruled the Kingdom of Armenia from 12 to 428 AD. The dynasty, a branch of the Arsacid dynasty of Parthia, reigned intermittently throughout the chaotic years following the fall of the Artaxiad dynasty until 62, when Tiridates I, brother of Parthian King Vologases I, secured Arsacid rule in Armenia as a client-king of the Roman Empire. However, he did not succeed in establishing his line on the throne, and various princes of different Arsacid lineages ruled until the accession of Vologases II, who succeeded in establishing his own line on the Armenian throne, which ruled the kingdom until the Sasanian Empire abolished it in 428.

gov: Province (marzpanate) of the Sasanian Empire, governed by a marzban
religion: Armenian Apostolic Christianity; Zoroastrian state religion of Persia
events: Vardan Mamikonian falls defending Christianity; commemorated as Vardanants.
facts: The 5th century is called the Golden Age of Armenian literature, when the Bible was translated.
entities.name: Persarmenia (Sasanian Armenia)
entities.summary: Sasanian Armenia, also known as Persian Armenia, Persarmenia and Armenian marzpanate, may either refer to the periods in which Armenia was under the suzerainty of the Sasanian Empire or specifically to the parts of Armenia under its control such as after the partition of 387, when parts of western Armenia were incorporated into the Eastern Roman Empire while the rest of Armenia came under Sasanian suzerainty but maintained its existing kingdom until 428.

religion: Armenian Christianity; Islam among rulers and garrisons
facts: Armenian princely families such as the Bagratunis kept local power under Arab governors.
entities.name: Arminiya
entities.summary: Arminiya, also known as the Ostikanate of Arminiya or the Emirate of Armenia, was a political and geographic designation given by the Muslim Arabs to the lands of Greater Armenia, Caucasian Iberia, and Caucasian Albania, following their conquest of these regions in the 7th century. Though the caliphs initially permitted an Armenian prince to represent the province of Arminiya in exchange for tribute and the Armenians' loyalty during times of war, Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan introduced direct Arab rule of the region, headed by a governor known as the ostikan with his capital in Dvin.

gov: Monarchy recognised by both the Caliph and the Byzantine Emperor
events: Ashot I recognised as king of Armenia
facts: Ani, the capital, was called "the city of 1001 churches"; estimates of its population run from 50,000 to over 100,000.
The architect Trdat, who built Ani Cathedral, also repaired the dome of Hagia Sophia after the 989 earthquake.
entities.name: Kingdom of Armenia (Bagratid)
entities.summary: Bagratid Armenia was an independent Armenian state established by Ashot I of the Bagratuni dynasty in the early 880s following nearly two centuries of foreign domination of Greater Armenia under Arab Umayyad and Abbasid rule. With each of the two contemporary powers in the region—the Abbasids and Byzantines—too preoccupied to concentrate their forces on subjugating the region, and with the dissipation of several of the Armenian nakharar noble families, Ashot succeeded in asserting himself as the leading figure of a movement to dislodge the Arabs from Armenia.

gov: Monarchy, allied with the Crusader states
events: Leo I crowned king of Cilicia
Mamluks capture Sis; the kingdom ends
facts: Armenian statehood continued here, on the Mediterranean coast of present-day Turkey, after the homeland fell.
entities.name: Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia
entities.summary: The Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, also known as Cilician Armenia, Lesser Armenia, Little Armenia or New Armenia, and formerly known as the Armenian Principality of Cilicia, was an Armenian state formed during the High Middle Ages by Armenian refugees fleeing the Seljuk invasion of Armenia. Located outside the Armenian Highlands and distinct from the Kingdom of Armenia of antiquity, it was centered in the Cilicia region, northwest of the Gulf of Alexandretta.

gov: Principality under the Kingdom of Georgia
religion: Armenian Apostolic and Georgian Orthodox Christianity
facts: The Zakarian brothers Zakare and Ivane were generals of Queen Tamar of Georgia.
entities.name: Zakarid Armenia
entities.summary: Zakarid Armenia alternatively known as the Zakarid Period, describes a historical period in the Middle Ages during which the Armenian vassals of the Kingdom of Georgia were ruled by the Zakarid-Mkhargrzeli dynasty. The city of Ani was the capital of the princedom. The Zakarids were vassals to the Bagrationi dynasty in Georgia, but frequently acted independently and at times titled themselves as kings. In 1236, they fell under the rule of the Mongol Empire as a vassal state with local autonomy.

facts: Timur's campaigns of the 1380s–1400s devastated the Armenian Highlands.
match: Emirate of the White Sheep Turks
entities.name: Armenia under the Ilkhanate and Turkmen dynasties
entities.summary: The Qara Qoyunlu or Kara Koyunlu, also known as the Black Sheep Turkomans, were a Turkoman, culturally Persianate, Muslim dynasty that ruled over the territory comprising present-day Azerbaijan, Armenia, northwestern Iran, eastern Turkey, and northeastern Iraq from about 1374 to 1468.

gov: Province of Safavid Persia, contested with the Ottomans
religion: Armenian Christianity; Shia Islam of the rulers
events: Great deportation of Armenians to Persia
facts: In 1604–05 Shah Abbas I deported much of the Armenian population of the Ararat plain to Persia; many settled in New Julfa, Isfahan.
entities.name: Armenia under Safavid Persia
entities.summary: The Guarded Domains of Iran, commonly called Safavid Iran, Safavid Persia or the Safavid Empire, was one of the largest and longest-lasting Iranian empires. It was ruled by the Safavid dynasty from 1501 to 1736, though some historians date its fall to 1722, when Isfahan fell to the Afghans. It is often considered the beginning of modern Iranian history, as well as one of the gunpowder empires.

gov: Khanate under the suzerainty of Afsharid, Zand and Qajar Iran
facts: On the eve of the Russian conquest, Muslims formed the majority of the khanate's population; Armenians became the majority within a few years after 1828.
entities.name: Erivan Khanate
entities.summary: The Erivan Khanate, also known as Chokhur-e Sa'd, was a khanate that was established in Afsharid Iran in the 18th century. It covered an area of roughly 19,500 km2, and corresponded to most of present-day central Armenia, the Iğdır Province and the Kars Province's Kağızman district in present-day Turkey and the Sharur and Sadarak districts of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic of present-day Azerbaijan.

events: Persia cedes the Erivan and Nakhichevan khanates to Russia.
Armenian Genocide in the Ottoman Empire
About 1 million or more Armenians are killed in 1915–1917; survivors flee to Russian Armenia.
facts: Russia gained the region from Persia in the Treaty of Turkmenchay (1828).
entities.name: Erivan Governorate (Russian Empire)
entities.summary: The Erivan Governorate was a province (guberniya) of the Caucasus Viceroyalty of the Russian Empire, with its centеr in Erivan. Its area was 27,830 sq. kilometеrs, roughly corresponding to what is now most of central Armenia, the Iğdır Province of Turkey, and the Nakhchivan exclave of Azerbaijan. At the end of the 19th century, it bordered the Tiflis Governorate to the north, the Elizavetpol Governorate to the east, the Kars Oblast to the west, and Persia and the Ottoman Empire to the south. Mount Ararat and the fertile Ararat Valley were included in the center of the province.

events: Armenian forces halt the Ottoman advance.
Red Army enters; Soviet rule begins
facts: Declared on 28 May 1918, the day remembered as Republic Day.
It granted women the vote in 1919, among the first countries to do so.
entities.name: First Republic of Armenia
entities.summary: The First Republic of Armenia, officially known at the time of its existence as the Republic of Armenia, was an independent Armenian state that existed from May 1918 to 2 December 1920 in the Armenian-populated territories of the former Russian Empire known as Eastern or Russian Armenia. The republic was established in May 1918, with its capital in the city of Yerevan, after the dissolution of the short-lived Transcaucasian Federation. It was the first Armenian state since the Middle Ages.

gov: Part of the Transcaucasian SFSR within the USSR
religion: Officially atheist state; the Armenian Church persisted
events: Mass demonstration in Yerevan on the genocide's 50th anniversary
facts: Soviet Armenia industrialised rapidly; Yerevan grew from about 30,000 people in 1920 to over a million by 1990.
The Spitak earthquake of December 1988 killed about 25,000 people.
entities.name: Armenian Soviet Socialist Republic
entities.summary: The Armenian Soviet Socialist Republic (ArSSR), also known as the Armenian SSR, Soviet Armenia, or simply Armenia, was one of the constituent republics of the Soviet Union, located in the Caucasus region of Eurasia. Soviet Armenia bordered the Soviet republics of Azerbaijan and Georgia and the independent states of Iran and Turkey. The capital of the republic was Yerevan, and it contained 37 districts (raions). Other major cities in the Armenian SSR included Leninakan, Kirovakan, Hrazdan, Ejmiatsin, and Kapan. The republic was governed by Communist Party of Armenia, a branch of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.

religion: Armenian Apostolic Church (over 90% of the population)
events: 1700th anniversary of Christianity as state religion
facts: Armenian has its own alphabet and forms its own branch of the Indo-European family.
Mount Ararat, the national symbol, lies just across the border in Turkey.
More Armenians live abroad than in Armenia itself; estimates of the diaspora run from 5 to 7 million.
entities.name: Republic of Armenia
entities.summary: Armenia, officially the Republic of Armenia, is a landlocked country in the Armenian highlands of West Asia. It is a part of the Caucasus region and is bordered by Turkey to the west, Georgia to the north, Azerbaijan to the east, and Iran and the Azerbaijani exclave of Nakhchivan to the south. Yerevan is the capital, largest city and financial center.

facts: In Greek myth, Colchis was the land of the Golden Fleece sought by Jason and the Argonauts.
entities.name: Colchis
entities.summary: In classical antiquity and Greco-Roman geography, Colchis was an exonym for the Georgian polity of Egrisi located on the eastern coast of the Black Sea, centered in present-day western Georgia also including the region of Abkhazia.

facts: King Mirian III adopted Christianity in the 330s after the preaching of St Nino.
entities.name: Kingdom of Iberia (Kartli)
entities.summary: In Greco-Roman geography, Iberia was an exonym for the Georgian kingdom of Kartli, known after its core province. The kingdom existed during Classical Antiquity and the Early Middle Ages, either as an independent state or as a dependent of larger empires, notably the Sassanid and Roman empires. Iberia, centered on present-day eastern Georgia, was bordered by Colchis in the west, Caucasian Albania in the east and Armenia in the south.

facts: Under Queen Tamar, Georgia reached its golden age; Rustaveli wrote "The Knight in the Panther's Skin".
entities.name: Kingdom of Georgia
entities.summary: The Kingdom of Georgia, also known as the Georgian Empire, was a medieval Eurasian monarchy that was founded in c. 1008 AD. It reached its Golden Age of political and economic strength during the reign of King David IV and Queen Tamar the Great from the 11th to 13th centuries. Georgia became one of the pre-eminent nations of the Christian East, and its pan-Caucasian empire and network of tributaries stretched from Eastern Europe to Anatolia and northern frontiers of Iran. At the height of its influence, Georgia also maintained several important religious centers abroad, such as the Bachkovo Monastery in Bulgaria, Monastery of the Cross in Jerusalem and the Monastery of Iviron in Greece. It is the principal historical precursor of present-day Georgia.

facts: Georgian has its own alphabet; its three scripts are on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
Qvevri winemaking in clay jars has an 8,000-year history in Georgia.
entities.name: Georgia
entities.summary: Georgia is a country in the Caucasus region on the east coast of the Black Sea. It is located at the intersection of Eastern Europe and West Asia and is generally regarded as part of Europe. It is bordered to the north and northeast by Russia; to the west by the Black Sea, to the south by Turkey and Armenia, and to the southeast by Azerbaijan. It has a population of 3.9 million, of which over a third live in Tbilisi, the capital and largest city. Georgians, who are native to the region and constitute the majority of the population, are ethno-linguistically distinct from their neighboring nations and primarily speak Georgian, a member of the small Kartvelian language family that has no relation to any other language family in the world.

facts: Baku was the world's leading oil producer around 1900.
entities.name: Republic of Azerbaijan
entities.summary: Azerbaijan, officially the Republic of Azerbaijan, is a landlocked country at the boundary of Western Asia and Eastern Europe. It is a part of the South Caucasus region and is bounded by the Caspian Sea to the east, Russia's republic of Dagestan to the north, Georgia to the northwest, Turkey and Armenia to the west, and Iran to the south. Baku is the capital and largest city.

facts: Unrelated to Albania in the Balkans; it lay in what is now Azerbaijan and southern Dagestan.
entities.name: Caucasian Albania
entities.summary: Caucasian Albania is a modern exonym for a former state located in ancient times in the Caucasus, mostly overlapping the region of present-day Azerbaijan. The modern endonyms for the area are Aghwank and Aluank, among the Udi people, who regard themselves as descended from the inhabitants of Caucasian Albania. However, its original endonym is unknown.

gov: League of city-states ruled by kings, later magistrates
facts: Etruscan is not Indo-European; it can be read, because its alphabet came from Greek, but is only partly understood.
Rome's last three kings were, by tradition, Etruscans.
entities.name: Etruscan civilisation
entities.summary: The Etruscans created a civilization in Etruria, in ancient Italy, with a common language and culture, and formed a federation of city-states. After adjacent lands had been conquered, its territory covered, at its greatest extent, roughly what is now Tuscany, western Umbria and northern Lazio, as well as what are now the Po Valley, Emilia-Romagna, south-eastern Lombardy, southern Veneto and western Campania.

events: Legend credits Romulus; archaeology shows settlement on the Palatine earlier.
facts: 21 April 753 BCE is the traditional founding date, worked out by Roman scholars centuries later.
entities.name: Roman Kingdom
entities.summary: The Roman Kingdom, also known as the Roman monarchy and the regal period of ancient Rome, was the earliest period of Roman history, when the city and its territory were ruled by kings. According to tradition, the Roman Kingdom began with the city's founding c. 753 BC, with settlements around the Palatine Hill along the river Tiber in central Italy, and ended with the overthrow of the kings and the establishment of the Roman Republic c. 509 BC.

gov: Republic led by two annually elected consuls and the Senate
facts: The census of 28 BCE counted about 4 million Roman citizens.
Rome fought three Punic Wars against Carthage, destroying it in 146 BCE.
Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE and was assassinated on the Ides of March, 44 BCE.
entities.name: Roman Republic
entities.summary: The Roman Republic was the era of classical Roman civilisation beginning with the overthrow of the Roman Kingdom and ending in 27 BC with the establishment of the Roman Empire following the War of Actium. During this period, Rome's control expanded from the city's immediate surroundings to hegemony over the entire Mediterranean world.

gov: Principate: an emperor behind republican forms
religion: Roman polytheism and the imperial cult
facts: At its height under Trajan (117 CE) the empire covered about 5 million km².
Rome itself probably reached about a million inhabitants in the 1st–2nd centuries CE.
In 395 the empire was permanently divided into western and eastern halves.
entities.name: Roman Empire
entities.summary: The Roman Empire was a state that dominated the Mediterranean and much of Europe, Western Asia, and North Africa during the classical period. The Roman Republic had previously conquered most of these territories, which later came under permanent single-person rule following Octavian's rise to power and the establishment of the Augustan Principate in 27 BC. By the late 3rd century AD, the empire had been divided many times. The Western Roman Empire collapsed in 476 AD, whereas the Eastern Roman Empire persisted until the fall of Constantinople in 1453.

gov: Gothic monarchy over a Roman administration
facts: Theodoric kept the Roman Senate and consuls; Boethius wrote "The Consolation of Philosophy" under his rule.
entities.name: Ostrogothic Kingdom
entities.summary: The Ostrogothic Kingdom, officially the Kingdom of Italy, was a barbarian kingdom established by the Germanic Ostrogoths that controlled Italy and neighbouring areas between 493 and 553. Led by Theodoric the Great, the Ostrogoths killed Odoacer, a Germanic soldier and erstwhile leader of the foederati. Odoacer had previously become the de facto ruler of Italy following Odoacer's deposition of Romulus Augustulus, the final emperor of the Western Roman Empire, in 476. Under Theodoric, the Ostrogothic kingdom reached its zenith, stretching from Southern France in the west to Western Serbia in the southeast. Most of the social institutions of the late Western Roman Empire were preserved during his rule. Theodoric called himself "King of the Goths and Romans", demonstrating his desire to be a leader for both peoples.

gov: Province of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire
facts: The Lombards invaded in 568 and held much of the peninsula; Rome stayed nominally Byzantine.
entities.name: Byzantine Italy
entities.summary: The Exarchate of Ravenna, also known as the Exarchate of Italy, was an exarchate of the Eastern Roman Empire comprising, between the 6th and 8th centuries, the territories under the jurisdiction of the exarch of Italy resident in Ravenna. The term is used in historiography in a double sense: "exarchate" in the strict sense denotes the territory under the direct jurisdiction of the exarch, i.e. the area of the capital Ravenna, but the term is mainly used to designate all the Byzantine territories in continental and peninsular Italy. According to the legal sources of the time, these territories constituted the so-called Provincia Italiae, on the basis of the fact that they too, until at least the end of the 7th century, fell under the jurisdiction of the exarch and were governed by duces or magistri militum under him.

gov: Elective theocratic monarchy ruled by the Pope
events: Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne in Rome
facts: The Donation of Pepin (756) created the Papal States from former Byzantine lands.
Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling between 1508 and 1512.
entities.name: Papal States
entities.summary: The Papal States, officially the State of the Church, were a conglomeration of territories on the Italian Peninsula under the direct sovereign rule of the pope from 756 to 1870. They were among the major Italian states from the 8th century until the unification of Italy, which took place between 1859 and 1870, culminating in their incorporation into the Kingdom of Italy.

gov: Fascist dictatorship under Mussolini, monarchy retained
facts: At unification only a small share of Italians, perhaps 2.5–10%, spoke standard Italian; most spoke regional languages.
entities.name: Kingdom of Italy
entities.summary: The Kingdom of Italy was a unitary state that existed from 17 March 1861, when Victor Emmanuel II, King of Sardinia, was proclaimed King of Italy, until 18 June 1946, when the monarchy was abolished, following civil discontent that led to an institutional referendum on 2 June, resulting in the establishment of the modern Italian Republic. The kingdom was established through the unification of several states over a decades-long process, called the Risorgimento. That process was influenced by House of Savoy-ruled Sardinia, which was one of Italy's legal predecessor states.

events: Treaty of Rome founds the European Economic Community
facts: Italy has more UNESCO World Heritage Sites than any other country except China.
The republic was chosen by referendum on 2 June 1946.
entities.name: Italian Republic
entities.summary: Italy, officially the Italian Republic, is a country in Southern and Western Europe. It consists of a peninsula, which extends into the Mediterranean Sea, with the Alps on its northern land border, as well as nearly 800 islands, notably Sicily and Sardinia. Italy shares land borders with France to the west; Switzerland and Austria to the north; Slovenia to the east; and the two enclaves of Vatican City and San Marino. It is the tenth-largest country in Europe by area, covering 301,340 km2 (116,350 sq mi), and the third-most populous member state of the European Union, with nearly 59 million inhabitants. Rome is the capital of Italy; other major cities include Milan, Naples, Turin, Palermo, Bologna, Florence, Genoa, Bari, and Venice.

facts: Linear B, deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952, proved the Mycenaeans wrote an early form of Greek.
entities.name: Mycenaean Greece
entities.summary: Mycenaean Greece, also called Mycenaean civilization, was the last phase of the Bronze Age in ancient Greece, spanning the period from approximately 1750 to 1050 BC. It represents the first advanced and distinctively Greek civilization in mainland Greece with its palatial states, urban organization, works of art, and writing system. The Mycenaeans were mainland Greek peoples who were likely stimulated by their contact with insular Minoan Crete and other Mediterranean cultures to develop a more sophisticated sociopolitical culture of their own. The most prominent site was Mycenae, after which the culture of this era is named. Other centers of power that emerged included Pylos, Tiryns, and Midea in the Peloponnese, Orchomenos, Thebes, and Athens in Central Greece, and Iolcos in Thessaly. Mycenaean settlements also appeared in Epirus, Macedonia, on islands in the Aegean Sea, on the south-west coast of Asia Minor, and on Cyprus, while Mycenaean-influenced settlements appeared in the Levant and Italy.

capitals: Athens, Sparta, Corinth, Thebes and hundreds of other poleis
gov: Athenian democracy alongside oligarchies like Sparta
facts: The first recorded Olympic Games were held in 776 BCE.
Cleisthenes' reforms of 508 BCE created Athenian democracy.
entities.name: Greek city-states
entities.summary: Polis is a term used to refer to Ancient Greek city-states. About 1,500 such states are known to have existed. Primarily located in Greece & Asia Minor, Greek poleis were founded throughout the Mediterranean and Black Sea regions.

facts: Alexander conquered the Persian Empire and reached the Indus within thirteen years.
entities.name: Kingdom of Macedon
entities.summary: Macedonia, also called Macedon, was an ancient kingdom on the periphery of Archaic and Classical Greece, which later became the dominant state of Hellenistic Greece. The kingdom was founded and initially ruled by the royal Argead dynasty, which was followed by the Antipatrid and Antigonid dynasties. Home to the ancient Macedonians, the earliest kingdom was centred on the northeastern part of the Greek peninsula, and bordered by Epirus to the southwest, Illyria to the northwest, Paeonia to the north, Thrace to the east and Thessaly to the south.

gov: Absolute monarchy with a vast bureaucracy
facts: Hagia Sophia, finished in 537, was the largest cathedral in the world for nearly a thousand years.
Its citizens called themselves Romans; "Byzantine" is a later scholarly label.
entities.name: Byzantine Empire
entities.summary: The Byzantine Empire, also known as the Eastern Roman Empire, was the continuation of the Eastern part of the Roman Empire centred on Constantinople during late antiquity and the Middle Ages. Having survived the fall of the Western Roman Empire in the 5th century AD, it endured until the fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Empire in 1453. The term 'Byzantine Empire' was coined only after its demise; its citizens used the term 'Roman Empire' and called themselves 'Romans'.

religion: Sunni Islam; millets for Christians and Jews
facts: At its peak in the late 1600s it ruled from Hungary to Yemen and Algeria to the Caspian.
entities.name: Ottoman Empire
entities.summary: The Ottoman Empire, also known historically as Turkey or the Turkish Empire, was a state that spanned much of Southeastern Europe, West Asia, and North Africa from the 14th century to the early 20th century, centred in modern-day Turkey. It also controlled parts of southeastern Central Europe between the early 16th and early 18th centuries.

facts: Independence was recognised in the London Protocol of 1830 after the war that began in 1821.
entities.name: Hellenic Republic
entities.summary: Greece, officially the Hellenic Republic, is a country located mostly on the Balkan peninsula of Southeastern Europe, with thousands of islands extending geographically to Asia Minor. It has a population of around 10 million. With nine regions and up to 227 inhabited islands, it has the longest coastline on the Mediterranean basin. The Ionian Sea is west of the mainland, Albania northwest, and North Macedonia and Bulgaria north. Turkey is east both by land and the Aegean Sea. The capital, Athens, is the largest Greek city, followed by Thessaloniki and Patras.

religion: Egyptian religion: Ra, Osiris, Isis, Amun
events: Among the oldest known peace treaties.
facts: The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for nearly 4,000 years.
Cleopatra VII lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
entities.name: Ancient Egypt
entities.summary: Ancient Egypt was a cradle of civilization concentrated along the lower reaches of the Nile River in the eastern part of North Africa. It emerged from prehistoric Egypt around 3150 BC, when Upper and Lower Egypt were united by Menes, who is believed by the majority of Egyptologists to have been the same person as Narmer. The history of ancient Egypt unfolded as a series of stable kingdoms interspersed by the "Intermediate Periods" of relative instability. These stable kingdoms existed in one of three periods: the Old Kingdom of the Early Bronze Age; the Middle Kingdom of the Middle Bronze Age; or the New Kingdom of the Late Bronze Age.

religion: Egyptian religion and Greek cults; Serapis
events: Death of Cleopatra; Rome annexes Egypt
facts: The Library of Alexandria made the city the intellectual capital of the Mediterranean.
The Rosetta Stone (196 BCE) repeats one decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek.
entities.name: Ptolemaic Kingdom
entities.summary: The Ptolemaic Kingdom or Ptolemaic Empire was an ancient Greek polity based in Egypt during the Hellenistic period. It was founded in 305 BC by the Macedonian Greek general Ptolemy I Soter, a companion of Alexander the Great, and was ruled by the Ptolemaic dynasty until the death of Cleopatra VII in 30 BC.

facts: About 95% of Egyptians live on the roughly 5% of land along the Nile valley and delta.
entities.name: Arab Republic of Egypt
entities.summary: Egypt, officially the Arab Republic of Egypt, is a country spanning the northeast corner of Africa and southwest corner of Asia via the Sinai Peninsula. It is bordered by the Mediterranean Sea to the north, Palestine and Israel to the northeast, the Red Sea to the east, Sudan and the Sahara to the south, and Libya to the west. The Gulf of Aqaba in the northeast separates Egypt from Jordan and Saudi Arabia. Cairo is the capital, largest city, and leading cultural centre, while Alexandria is the second-largest city and an important hub of industry and tourism. With over 107 million inhabitants, Egypt is the most populous country in the Arab world, third-most populous country in Africa, and 15th-most populated in the world.

facts: Banpo, near Xi'an, is a well-preserved Yangshao village with painted pottery.
Millet, not rice, was the staple of these early northern Chinese farmers.
entities.name: Yangshao culture
entities.summary: The Yangshao culture was a Neolithic culture that existed extensively along the middle reaches of the Yellow River in China from around 5000 BC to 3000 BC. The Yangshao culture saw social and technological development in the region, with advancements in agriculture, architecture, and crafts.

facts: Longshan potters made eggshell-thin black ware on fast wheels.
entities.name: Longshan culture
entities.summary: The Longshan culture, also sometimes referred to as the Black Pottery Culture, was a late Neolithic culture in the middle and lower Yellow River valley areas of northern China from about 3000 to 1900 BC. The first archaeological find of this culture took place at the Chengziya Archaeological Site in 1928, with the first excavations in 1930 and 1931. The culture is named after the nearby modern town of Longshan in Zhangqiu, Shandong. The culture is noted for its highly polished black pottery.

gov: Hereditary dynasty described in later texts
facts: No contemporary writing of the Xia survives; some archaeologists link it to the Erlitou culture, others doubt it existed.
entities.name: Xia dynasty
entities.summary: The Xia dynasty is the first dynasty in traditional Chinese historiography. Some scholars, especially Western historians and Sinologists, consider the Xia dynasty legendary or at least unsubstantiated, while a majority of Chinese archeologists consider it historical and identify it with the archaeological Erlitou culture. According to tradition, it was established by the likely legendary figure Yu the Great, after Shun, the last of the Five Emperors, gave the throne to him. In traditional historiography, the Xia dynasty was succeeded by the Shang dynasty.

gov: Kingship legitimised by ancestor worship and divination
religion: Ancestor veneration; oracle-bone divination to the high god Di
facts: Oracle bones from Anyang are the earliest known Chinese writing, about 3,200 years old.
Fu Hao, a wife of King Wu Ding, led armies; her intact tomb was found in 1976.
entities.name: Shang dynasty
entities.summary: The Shang dynasty, also known as the Yin dynasty, was a Chinese royal dynasty that ruled in the Yellow River valley during the 2nd millennium BC, traditionally succeeding the Xia dynasty and followed by the Western Zhou dynasty. The classic account of the Shang comes from texts such as the Book of Documents, Bamboo Annals and Shiji. Modern scholarship dates the dynasty between the 16th and 11th centuries BC, with more agreement surrounding the end date than beginning date.

gov: Feudal monarchy under the Mandate of Heaven
religion: Ancestor worship, Heaven (Tian); Confucian and Daoist thought emerge
events: Battle of Muye: Zhou overthrows Shang
First precisely dated year in Chinese history
Zhou court moves east to Luoyang
facts: China's continuous dated history begins in 841 BCE.
Confucius (551–479 BCE) taught in the state of Lu.
names: Eastern Zhou: Spring and Autumn period
entities.name: Zhou dynasty
entities.summary: The Zhou dynasty was a royal dynasty of China that existed for 790 years from c. 1046 BC until 256 BC, the longest span of any dynasty in Chinese history. During the Western Zhou period, the royal house, surnamed Ji, had military control over territories centered on the Wei River valley and North China Plain. Even as Zhou suzerainty became increasingly ceremonial over the following Eastern Zhou period (771–256 BC), the political system created by the Zhou royal house survived in some form for several additional centuries. A date of 1046 BC for the Zhou's establishment is supported by the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project and David Pankenier, after David Nivison and Edward L. Shaughnessy had previously dated the establishment to 1045 BC.

gov: Centralised Legalist empire divided into commanderies
rulers: Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor
facts: The First Emperor standardised script, coins, weights and axle widths.
His tomb is guarded by the Terracotta Army, about 8,000 figures found in 1974.
entities.name: Qin dynasty
entities.summary: The Qin dynasty was the first imperial dynasty of China. It is named for its progenitor state of Qin, a fief of the confederal Zhou dynasty. Beginning in 230 BC, the Qin under King Ying Zheng engaged in a series of wars conquering each of the rival states that had previously pledged fealty to the Zhou. This culminated in 221 BC with the successful unification of China. The Qin then assumed an imperial prerogative – with Ying Zheng declaring himself to be Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China, and bringing an end to the Warring States period. This state of affairs lasted until 206 BC, when the dynasty collapsed in the years following Qin Shi Huang's death. The Qin dynasty's 14-year existence was the shortest of any major dynasty in Chinese history, with only two emperors. However, the succeeding Han dynasty largely continued the military and administrative practices instituted by the Qin; as a result, the Qin have been credited as the originators of the Chinese imperial system that would endure in some form until the Xinhai Revolution in 1911.

gov: Imperial bureaucracy, Confucian state ideology from Emperor Wu
religion: Confucianism, Daoism, folk religion; Buddhism arrives in the 1st century CE
events: Zhang Qian's mission to Central Asia opens the Silk Road
facts: The census of 2 CE counted 57.7 million people, one of the oldest surviving censuses.
Cai Lun is credited with improving papermaking in 105 CE.
The Han Chinese, China's largest ethnic group, are named after this dynasty.
entities.name: Han dynasty
entities.summary: The Han dynasty was an imperial dynasty of China established by Liu Bang, and preceded by the short-lived Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) and the interregnum known as the Chu–Han Contention (206–202 BC). It was succeeded by the Three Kingdoms period (220–280 AD) and also briefly interrupted by the Xin dynasty (9–23 AD) established by the usurping regent Wang Mang. It is thus separated into two periods—the Western Han and the Eastern Han (25–220 AD). The Han dynasty is considered a golden age in Chinese history, impacting Chinese identity in later periods. The majority ethnic group of modern China refer to themselves as the "Han people", while spoken Chinese and written Chinese are referred to respectively as the "Han language" and "Han characters".

gov: Three rival kingdoms: Wei, Shu, Wu
facts: The period inspired the novel "Romance of the Three Kingdoms", written over a thousand years later.
entities.name: Three Kingdoms, Jin and the Northern and Southern dynasties
entities.summary: Six Dynasties is a collective term for six Han-ruled Chinese dynasties that existed from the early 3rd century AD to the late 6th century AD, between the end of the Eastern Han dynasty and the beginning of the Sui dynasty. The Six Dynasties period overlapped with the era of the Sixteen Kingdoms, a chaotic warring period in northern China after the collapse of the Western Jin dynasty, as well as the Northern and Southern dynasties period. The terms "Wei, Jin, Southern and Northern dynasties" (魏晉南北朝) and "Three Kingdoms, Two Jins, Southern and Northern dynasties" (三國兩晉南北朝) are also used by Chinese historians to refer to the same historical era as the Six Dynasties, although the three terms do not refer to the same group of dynasties.

facts: The Sui built the Grand Canal linking the Yellow and Yangtze rivers.
It began the imperial examination system that lasted until 1905.
entities.name: Sui dynasty
entities.summary: The Sui dynasty was a Chinese imperial dynasty that ruled from 581 to 618 AD. The re-unification of China proper under the Sui brought the Northern and Southern dynasties era to a close, ending a prolonged period of political division since the War of the Eight Princes. The Sui endeavoured to rebuild the state, re-establishing and reforming many imperial institutions; in so doing, the Sui laid much of the foundation for the subsequent Tang dynasty, which after toppling the Sui would ultimately preside over a new golden age in Chinese history. Often compared to the Qin dynasty (221–206 BC), the Sui likewise unified China after a prolonged period of division, undertook wide-ranging reforms and construction projects to consolidate state power, and collapsed after a brief period.

rulers: Wu Zetian, China's only empress regnant
religion: Buddhism, Daoism, Confucianism; Christianity and Islam present in Chang'an
facts: Chang'an was among the largest cities in the world, with perhaps a million people.
The Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest dated printed book.
entities.name: Tang dynasty
entities.summary: The Tang dynasty was an imperial dynasty of China that ruled from 618 to 907, with an interregnum between 690 and 705. It was preceded by the Sui dynasty and followed by the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. Historians generally regard the Tang as a high point of Chinese civilisation, and a golden age of cosmopolitan culture. Tang territory, acquired through the military campaigns of its early rulers, surpassed that of the Han dynasty.

events: Battle of Yamen: Mongols complete the conquest
facts: The Song issued the world's first government paper money.
Gunpowder weapons, the magnetic compass and movable type all appear in Song China.
entities.name: Song dynasty
entities.summary: The Song dynasty was an imperial dynasty of China that ruled from 960 to 1279. The dynasty was founded by Emperor Taizu of Song, who usurped the throne of the Later Zhou dynasty and went on to conquer the rest of the Ten Kingdoms, ending the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. The Song often came into conflict with the contemporaneous Liao, Western Xia, and Jin dynasties in northern China. After retreating to southern China following attacks by the Jin dynasty, the Song was eventually conquered by the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty.

gov: Mongol-led empire, part of the wider Mongol world
religion: Tibetan Buddhism favoured at court; all faiths tolerated
facts: Marco Polo described Kublai Khan's court in the 1270s–1290s.
entities.name: Yuan dynasty
entities.summary: The Yuan dynasty, officially the Great Yuan, was a Mongol-led imperial dynasty of China and a successor state to the Mongol Empire after its division. It was established by Kublai, the fifth khagan-emperor of the Mongol Empire from the Borjigin clan, and lasted from 1271 to 1368 CE. In Chinese history, the Yuan dynasty followed the Song dynasty and preceded the Ming dynasty.

facts: The Forbidden City was completed in 1420.
Zheng He led seven voyages as far as East Africa.
Most of the Great Wall visible today was built under the Ming.
entities.name: Ming dynasty
entities.summary: The Ming dynasty, officially the Great Ming, was an imperial dynasty of China that ruled from 1368 to 1644, following the collapse of the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty. The Ming was the last imperial dynasty of China ruled by the Han people, the majority ethnic group in China. Although the primary capital of Beijing fell in 1644 to a rebellion led by Li Zicheng, numerous rump regimes ruled by remnants of the Ming imperial family, collectively called the Southern Ming, survived until 1662.

facts: At its height the Qing ruled about 13 million km², the largest territory of any Chinese dynasty.
The Taiping Rebellion (1850–64) killed perhaps 20–30 million people.
entities.name: Qing dynasty
entities.summary: The Qing dynasty, officially the Great Qing, also known as the Qing Empire or Qing China, was a Manchu-led imperial dynasty of China and an early modern empire in East Asia which existed from 1636/1644 to 1912. The last imperial dynasty in Chinese history, the Qing dynasty was preceded by the Ming dynasty and succeeded by the Republic of China. At the height of its power, the empire stretched from the Sea of Japan in the east to the Pamir Mountains in the west, and from the Mongolian Plateau in the north to the South China Sea in the south. Originally emerging from the Later Jin dynasty founded in 1616 and proclaimed in Shenyang in 1636, the dynasty seized control of the Ming capital Beijing and North China in 1644, traditionally considered the start of the dynasty's rule. The dynasty lasted until the Xinhai Revolution of October 1911 led to the abdication of the last emperor in February 1912. The multi-ethnic Qing dynasty assembled the territorial base for modern China. The Qing controlled the most territory of any dynasty in Chinese history, and in 1790 was the fourth-largest empire in world history to that point. It was also the most populous state at the time, with over 426 million citizens in 1907.

entities.name: Republic of China
entities.summary: The Republic of China established its governance over mainland China on 1 January 1912 following the Xinhai Revolution, which overthrew the Manchu-led Qing dynasty and ended China's imperial history. The Beiyang government in Beijing was the internationally recognized government of the ROC from 1912 to 1928, with regional warlords occupying parts of the country after the death of Beiyang leader Yuan Shikai in 1916. In 1926, the Kuomintang (KMT) launched the Northern Expedition, which eventually reunified the country in 1928. The KMT established the Nationalist government and governed the ROC as a one-party state with Nanjing as the capital. In 1949, the KMT was defeated in the Chinese Civil War by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and the ROC government retreated to Taiwan, where it remains to this date. The ROC is recorded as a founding member of both the League of Nations and the United Nations. It claimed 11.4 million km2 (4.4 million sq mi) of territory, and its population of 541 million in 1949 made it the most populous country in the world.

gov: One-party socialist republic led by the Communist Party
religion: Officially atheist state; Buddhism, Daoism and folk religion widespread
facts: China uses a single time zone although it spans about five geographical ones.
The Three Gorges Dam is the world's largest power station by capacity.
entities.name: People's Republic of China
entities.summary: China, officially the People's Republic of China (PRC), is a country in East Asia. It is divided into 33 province-level divisions, including two special administrative regions. Beijing is the capital, while Shanghai is the most populous city by urban area. Its geography features the Central Plain, major rivers such as the Yangtze and Yellow River, deserts, subtropical and temperate forests, plateaus, and mountain ranges such as the Himalayas. It is the world's second-most populous country after India, with a population exceeding 1.4 billion. Covering 9.6 million square kilometers (3,700,000 sq mi), it is the third largest country by area.

events: Maize domesticated from teosinte in the Balsas valley
facts: Maize was domesticated from the wild grass teosinte in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago.
entities.name: Archaic Mesoamerican foragers and early farmers
entities.summary: In the classification of the archaeological cultures of North America, the Archaic period in North America, taken to last from around 8000 to 1000 BC in the sequence of North American pre-Columbian cultural stages, is a period defined by the archaic stage of cultural development. The Archaic stage is characterized by subsistence economies supported through the exploitation of nuts, seeds, and shellfish. As its ending is defined by the adoption of sedentary farming, this date can vary significantly across the Americas.

gov: Chiefdoms or early states led by rulers
religion: Were-jaguar and maize deities; ritual ball game
facts: The Olmec carved colossal stone heads up to 3.4 m tall, probably portraits of rulers.
The rubber balls of their ball game are among the oldest known, around 1600 BCE.
entities.name: Olmec civilisation
entities.summary: The Olmecs or Olmec were an early major Mesoamerican civilization, flourishing in the modern-day Mexican states of Veracruz and Tabasco from roughly 1200 to 400 BC during Mesoamerica's formative period. They are known as one of the cradles of civilization. The Olmecs were initially centered at the site of their development in San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán, but moved to La Venta in the 10th century BC following the decline of San Lorenzo. By about 400 BC the major centres of the Olmec civilization had been abandoned, and the population of the eastern half of the Olmec heartland dropped precipitously. The settlement density in that area remained much lower than during the height of Olmec dominance, and only intermittent occupation is evident until much later. Although the Olmec cultural style waned, elements of their tradition lived on in successor societies.

capitals: Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, Copán and other city-states
gov: Rival city-states ruled by divine kings (k'uhul ajaw)
religion: Maya religion: Itzamna, Chaak, the Maize God; calendrical ritual
events: Earliest dated Long Count stela at Tikal
Collapse of the southern lowland cities
facts: Maya script is a full writing system; most inscriptions can now be read.
Maya astronomers tracked the cycles of Venus with great accuracy, recorded in the Dresden Codex.
The last independent Maya kingdom, Nojpetén, fell to Spain in 1697.
entities.name: Maya civilisation
entities.summary: The Maya civilization was a Mesoamerican civilization that existed from antiquity to the early modern period. Known by its ancient temples and glyphs (script), the civilization is also noted for its art, architecture, mathematics, calendar, and astronomical system. The Maya script is the most sophisticated and highly developed writing system in the pre-Columbian Americas.

gov: City-state; its form of rule is debated
facts: With perhaps 100,000–150,000 people, it was among the largest cities in the world around 450 CE.
Its real name and language are unknown; "Teotihuacan" is a later Aztec name meaning "place where the gods were born".
entities.name: Teotihuacan
entities.summary: Teotihuacan is an ancient Mesoamerican city located in a sub-valley of the Valley of Mexico, which is located in the State of Mexico, 40 kilometers (25 mi) northeast of modern-day Mexico City.

facts: The Aztecs revered the Toltecs as the source of civilisation, so much of their history is legend.
entities.name: Toltec state
entities.summary: The Toltec culture was a pre-Columbian Mesoamerican culture that ruled a state centered in Tula, Hidalgo, Mexico, during the Epiclassic and the early Post-Classic period of Mesoamerican chronology, reaching prominence from 950 to 1150 AD. The later Aztec culture considered the Toltec to be their intellectual and cultural predecessors and described Toltec culture emanating from Tōllān as the epitome of civilization. In the Nahuatl language the word Tōltēkatl (singular) or Tōltēkah (plural) came to take on the meaning "artisan". The Aztec oral and pictographic tradition also described the history of the Toltec Empire, giving lists of rulers and their exploits.

gov: Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan collecting tribute
facts: Tenochtitlan was built on an island in Lake Texcoco, with causeways and floating chinampa gardens.
Words like chocolate, tomato and avocado come from Nahuatl.
entities.name: Aztec Empire (Triple Alliance)
entities.summary: The Aztec Empire, also known as the Triple Alliance or historiographically as the Tenochca Empire but most accurately known as the Mexica, was an alliance of three Nahua city-states: Mexico-Tenochtitlan, Tetzcoco, and Tlacopan. These three city-states ruled that area in and around the Valley of Mexico from 1428 until the combined forces of the Spanish conquistadores and their native allies who ruled under Hernán Cortés defeated them in 1521. Its people and civil society are historiographically referred to as the Aztecs or the Culhua-Mexica.

gov: Colonial viceroyalty of the Spanish Crown
facts: Epidemics such as smallpox and cocoliztli killed a large majority of the Indigenous population within a century.
Silver from Zacatecas and Guanajuato, minted as pieces of eight, became a global currency.
entities.name: Viceroyalty of New Spain
entities.summary: New Spain, officially the Viceroyalty of New Spain, originally the Kingdom of New Spain, was an integral territorial entity of the Spanish Empire, established by Habsburg Spain. It was one of several domains established during the Spanish conquest of the Americas, and had its capital in Mexico City. Its jurisdiction comprised a large area of the southern and western portions of North America, mainly what became Mexico and the Southwestern United States, but also California, Florida and Louisiana; Central America ; the Caribbean like Hispaniola and Martinique, and northern parts of South America, even Colombia; several Pacific archipelagos, including the Philippines and Guam. Additional Asian colonies included "Spanish Formosa", on the island of Taiwan.

events: Mexico cedes about half its territory to the United States.
facts: Mexico recognises 68 Indigenous languages alongside Spanish.
It is home to the largest Spanish-speaking population in the world.
entities.name: United Mexican States
entities.summary: Mexico, officially the United Mexican States, is a country in North America. It is the northernmost country in Latin America, bordering the United States of America to the north and Guatemala and Belize to the southeast, while having maritime boundaries with the Pacific Ocean to the west, the Caribbean Sea to the southeast, and the Gulf of Mexico to the east. Mexico covers 1,972,550 km2, and is the thirteenth-largest country in the world by land area. With a population around 131 million as of 2025, Mexico is the tenth-most populous country in the world and is home to the largest number of native Spanish speakers. Mexico City is the capital and largest city in Mexico, which ranks among the most populous metropolitan areas in the world.

facts: Stonehenge was built in stages between about 3000 and 1500 BCE.
Ancient DNA shows the Beaker people replaced around 90% of Britain's gene pool after 2500 BCE.
entities.name: Neolithic and Bronze Age Britain
entities.summary: Several species of humans have intermittently occupied Great Britain for almost a million years. The earliest evidence of human occupation around 900,000 years ago is at Happisburgh on the Norfolk coast, with stone tools and now destroyed footprints possibly made by Homo antecessor or Homo erectus. The oldest human fossils, around 480,000 years old, are of "Boxgrove Man" from the Boxgrove site in Sussex. Until that time, Britain had been permanently connected to the Continent by a chalk ridge between South East England and northern France called the Weald–Artois Anticline, but during the Anglian Glaciation around 425,000 years ago a megaflood broke through the ridge, and Britain became increasingly isolated from continental Europe, until fully becoming an island around 130,000 years ago.

facts: Hill forts like Maiden Castle were large fortified settlements.
Julius Caesar raided Britain in 55 and 54 BCE but did not conquer it.
entities.name: Iron Age Britons
entities.summary: The Britons, also known as Celtic Britons or ancient Britons, were the Celtic people who inhabited Great Britain from at least the British Iron Age until the High Middle Ages, at which point they diverged into the Welsh, Cornish, and Bretons. They spoke Common Brittonic, the ancestor of the modern Brittonic languages.

facts: Hadrian's Wall, begun in 122, ran 117 km across northern Britain.
Boudica of the Iceni burned Londinium in her revolt of 60 or 61 CE.
entities.name: Roman Britain
entities.summary: Roman Britain was the territory that became the Roman province of Britannia after the Roman conquest of Britain, consisting of a large part of the island of Great Britain. The occupation lasted from 43 AD to 410 AD.

gov: Rival kingdoms: Wessex, Mercia, Northumbria, East Anglia, Kent, Essex, Sussex
events: Alfred defeats the Danes at Edington
facts: The Sutton Hoo ship burial (c. 625) held the richest treasure found in England.
From 865 the Viking Great Heathen Army conquered much of England.
entities.name: Anglo-Saxon kingdoms
entities.summary: The Heptarchy was the division of Anglo-Saxon England between the sixth and eighth centuries into petty kingdoms, conventionally the seven kingdoms of East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Mercia, Northumbria, Sussex, and Wessex. The term originated with the twelfth-century historian Henry of Huntingdon and has been widely used ever since, but it has been questioned by historians as the number of kingdoms fluctuated, and there was never a time when the territory of the Anglo-Saxons was divided into seven kingdoms, each ruled by one king. The period of petty kingdoms came to an end in the eighth century, when England was divided into the four dominant kingdoms of East Anglia, Mercia, Northumbria, and Wessex.

gov: Monarchy limited by Magna Carta and Parliament
facts: The Domesday Book of 1086 surveyed landholdings across England.
The Black Death of 1348–49 killed perhaps 40% or more of England's people.
entities.name: Kingdom of England
entities.summary: The Kingdom of England was a sovereign state on the island of Great Britain from 927, when all of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms were united under the rule of Æthelstan, until 1 May 1707, when it relinquished its sovereignty along with Scotland to form the Kingdom of Great Britain, which would later become the United Kingdom. The Kingdom of England was among the most powerful states in Europe during the medieval and early modern periods.

entities.name: Kingdom of Scotland
entities.summary: The Kingdom of Scotland was a sovereign state in northwest Europe, traditionally said to have been founded in 843. Its territories expanded and shrank, but it came to occupy the northern third of the island of Great Britain, sharing a land border to the south with the Kingdom of England. During the Middle Ages, Scotland engaged in intermittent conflict with England, most prominently the Wars of Scottish Independence, which saw the Scots maintain and assert their independence from the English. Following Scotland's annexation of the Hebrides and the Northern Isles from Norway in 1266 and 1472 respectively, and England's capture of Berwick in 1482, the territory of the Kingdom of Scotland corresponded to that of modern-day Scotland, bounded by the North Sea to the east, the Atlantic Ocean to the north and west, and the North Channel and Irish Sea to the southwest.

religion: Christianity (Church of England, Church of Scotland); increasingly secular
facts: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain, powered by coal and steam.
Around 1920 the British Empire covered about a quarter of the world's land.
match: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
names: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
entities.name: United Kingdom
entities.summary: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the United Kingdom (UK) or Britain, is a country in Northwestern Europe, off the coast of the continental mainland. It comprises England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, with a population of over 69 million in 2025. The UK includes the island of Great Britain, the north-eastern part of the island of Ireland, and most of the smaller islands within the British Isles, covering 94,354 square miles (244,376 km2). It shares a land border with the Republic of Ireland and is surrounded by the Atlantic Ocean, the North Sea, the English Channel, the Celtic Sea and the Irish Sea, while maintaining sovereignty over the Crown Dependencies and the British Overseas Territories. The capital and largest city of England and the UK is London; Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast are the national capitals of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, respectively.

gov: Dominion, later state with ambiguous status
facts: Irish is the first official language under the constitution, though English is the everyday language of most.
entities.name: Ireland
entities.summary: Ireland, also known as the Republic of Ireland, is a country in Northwestern Europe. It consists of 26 of the 32 counties of the island of Ireland, with a population of about 5.4 million. Its capital and largest city is Dublin, on the eastern side of the island, with a population of over 1.5 million. The sovereign state shares its only land border with Northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom. It is otherwise surrounded by the Atlantic Ocean, with the Celtic Sea to the south, St George's Channel to the south-east and the Irish Sea to the east. It is a unitary, parliamentary republic. The legislature, the Oireachtas, consists of a lower house, Dáil Éireann; an upper house, Seanad Éireann; and an elected president who serves as the largely ceremonial head of state, but with some important powers and duties. The head of government is the Taoiseach, elected by the Dáil and appointed by the president, who appoints other government ministers.

gov: Many small kingdoms under provincial and High Kings
facts: The Book of Kells was made around 800 in a Columban monastery.
Vikings founded Dublin as a longphort in 841.
entities.name: Gaelic Ireland
entities.summary: Gaelic Ireland was the Gaelic political and social order, and associated culture, that existed in Ireland from the late prehistoric era until the 17th century. It comprised the whole island before Anglo-Normans conquered parts of Ireland in the 1170s. Thereafter, it comprised that part of the country not under foreign dominion at a given time. For most of its history, Gaelic Ireland was a "patchwork" hierarchy of territories ruled by a hierarchy of kings or chiefs, who were chosen or elected through tanistry. Warfare between these territories was common. Traditionally, a powerful ruler like Niall of the Nine Hostages where acknowledged as High King of Ireland. Society was made up of clans and, like the rest of Europe, was structured hierarchically according to class. Throughout this period, the economy was mainly pastoral and money was generally not used. A Gaelic Irish style of dress, music, dance, sport and art can be identified, with Irish art later merging with Anglo-Saxon styles to create Insular art.

events.title: Chicxulub impact
events.text: An asteroid about 10 km across strikes the Yucatán, triggering the extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs.

events.title: Earliest Homo sapiens fossils
events.text: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, dated to about 300,000 years ago.

events.title: Toba supereruption
events.text: The largest volcanic eruption of the last 2 million years, in Sumatra. Its effect on early humans is debated.

events.title: Lascaux cave paintings
events.text: Hundreds of animals painted on cave walls in southwestern France.

events.title: Göbekli Tepe
events.text: Monumental carved pillars raised by hunter-gatherers, among the oldest known megaliths.

events.title: Walls of Jericho
events.text: One of the oldest walled settlements, with a stone tower about 8.5 m tall.

events.title: Çatalhöyük
events.text: A dense Neolithic town of mud-brick houses entered through the roofs.

events.title: Oldest known winery
events.text: Wine is pressed and fermented in Areni-1 cave, Armenia.

events.title: Writing in Uruk
events.text: Proto-cuneiform tablets appear in Uruk, Mesopotamia.

events.title: Egypt unified
events.text: Upper and Lower Egypt are joined under one king.

events.title: Stonehenge begun
events.text: The first earthwork enclosure is dug; the great sarsens follow around 2500 BCE.

events.title: Great Pyramid completed
events.text: Built for the pharaoh Khufu at Giza.

events.title: Code of Hammurabi
events.text: One of the earliest written law codes, issued in Babylon.

events.title: Battle of Kadesh
events.text: Egypt and the Hittites fight one of the largest chariot battles known.

events.title: Oracle-bone script
events.text: The earliest known Chinese writing, at the Shang capital Yin (Anyang).

events.title: Erebuni founded
events.text: King Argishti I of Urartu founds the fortress that becomes Yerevan.

events.title: First recorded Olympic Games
events.text: Held at Olympia in honour of Zeus.

events.title: Founding of Rome (traditional)
events.text: The traditional date, set by later Roman scholars.

events.title: Battle of Marathon
events.text: Athens defeats the first Persian invasion of Greece.

events.title: Battle of Gaugamela
events.text: Alexander defeats Darius III; the Achaemenid Empire falls.

events.title: Qin unifies China
events.text: Ying Zheng proclaims himself the First Emperor.

events.title: Battle of Cannae
events.text: Hannibal destroys a much larger Roman army.

events.title: Artaxata founded
events.text: Artaxias I builds a new capital on the Araxes.

events.title: Battle of Tigranocerta
events.text: Lucullus defeats Tigranes the Great.

events.title: Assassination of Julius Caesar
events.text: Stabbed in the Theatre of Pompey on the Ides of March.

events.title: Vesuvius buries Pompeii
events.text: Pompeii and Herculaneum are buried under ash and pyroclastic flows.

events.title: Hadrian's Wall begun
events.text: A frontier wall across northern Britain.

events.title: Pyramid of the Sun
events.text: Teotihuacan completes one of the largest pyramids in the Americas.

events.title: Armenia adopts Christianity
events.text: Traditionally the first state to do so; some scholars prefer 314.

events.title: Constantinople dedicated
events.text: Constantine makes Byzantium the new Roman capital.

events.title: Armenian alphabet
events.text: Mesrop Mashtots creates the 36-letter alphabet.

events.title: Last western emperor deposed
events.text: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna.

events.title: Hagia Sophia consecrated
events.text: Justinian's great church in Constantinople.

events.title: Tikal defeats Calakmul
events.text: Jasaw Chan Kʼawiil I restores Tikal's power.

events.title: Vikings raid Lindisfarne
events.text: Often taken as the start of the Viking Age in Britain.

events.title: Charlemagne crowned emperor
events.text: Pope Leo III crowns him in St Peter's, Rome.

events.title: Ani becomes capital
events.text: Ashot III moves the Bagratid capital to Ani.

events.title: Battle of Hastings
events.text: William of Normandy defeats Harold II.

events.title: Battle of Manzikert
events.text: The Seljuks defeat Byzantium, opening Anatolia to Turkic settlement.

events.title: Magna Carta
events.text: Sealed by King John at Runnymede.

events.title: Yuan dynasty proclaimed
events.text: Kublai Khan rules from Khanbaliq (Beijing).

events.title: Tenochtitlan founded
events.text: Traditional date for the Mexica capital on Lake Texcoco.

events.title: Black Death reaches Europe
events.text: Plague arrives at Messina and Caffa; it kills perhaps a third of Europe.

events.title: Zheng He's first voyage
events.text: The Ming treasure fleet sails for the Indian Ocean.

events.title: Fall of Constantinople
events.text: Mehmed II takes the city; the Byzantine Empire ends.

events.title: Columbus reaches the Caribbean
events.text: Landfall in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492.

events.title: Fall of Tenochtitlan
events.text: Cortés and his Indigenous allies take the Aztec capital.

events.title: Spanish Armada defeated
events.text: Storms and the English fleet wreck the invasion.

events.title: Treaty of Turkmenchay
events.text: Persia cedes the Erivan and Nakhichevan khanates to Russia.

events.title: First Opium War
events.text: Britain wars on Qing China over the opium trade.

events.title: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
events.text: Mexico cedes about half its territory to the United States.

events.title: Xinhai Revolution
events.text: The Wuchang Uprising ends two thousand years of imperial rule.

events.title: Assassination in Sarajevo
events.text: Archduke Franz Ferdinand is shot; the First World War follows.

events.title: Armenian Genocide begins
events.text: Mass deportations and killings of Armenians in the Ottoman Empire, 1915–1917.

events.title: Battle of Sardarapat
events.text: Armenian forces halt the Ottoman advance; independence follows.

events.title: Atomic bombings
events.text: Hiroshima and Nagasaki; Japan surrenders weeks later.

events.title: People's Republic proclaimed
events.text: Mao Zedong proclaims the PRC in Tiananmen Square.

events.title: Spitak earthquake
events.text: About 25,000 people die in northern Armenia.

events.title: Berlin Wall falls
events.text: East Germany opens its borders on 9 November 1989.

events.title: Armenia votes for independence
events.text: Referendum of 21 September 1991.

routes.name: Silk Road
routes.text: Overland trade linking Han China with Central Asia, Persia and the Mediterranean.

routes.name: Silk Road (Caucasus branch)
routes.text: A northern branch through Armenia and Georgia to the Black Sea.

routes.name: Columbian exchange: Atlantic crossing
routes.text: Crops, animals, people and diseases cross the Atlantic in both directions.

routes.name: Manila galleons
routes.text: Spanish ships carry silver from Acapulco to Manila and silk and porcelain back.

routes.name: Mongol expansion westward
routes.text: Mongol armies sweep from Karakorum to Persia, the Caucasus and Eastern Europe.

routes.name: Mongol conquest of China
routes.text: From the Jin north to the fall of the Southern Song.

routes.name: Zheng He's voyages
routes.text: Seven Ming expeditions across the Indian Ocean.
